articles.title: Grok Bot se integra al sistema bancario para actuar como un asistente de finanzas personales
articles.text:
Grok Bot, el asistente de inteligencia artificial de xAI, la empresa de Elon Musk, habilitó una función llamada Finance que permite vincular cuentas bancarias, tarjetas de crédito y cuentas de inversión directamente a la plataforma para que la IA las administre.
La cuenta oficial de Grok Bot en la red social X anunció el 26 de septiembre que los usuarios ya pueden enlazar sus cuentas y luego pedirle al asistente que ayude a gestionar sus gastos e inversiones. “Grok Bot ahora se conecta a tus finanzas”, escribió la cuenta oficial del producto.
PUBLICIDAD
Musk amplificó el anuncio esa misma tarde en su propia cuenta, con el mensaje “Grok Bot puede administrar tus finanzas”. La publicación del magnate sumó más de 300.000 impresiones en pocas horas, según registró el sitio financiero 24/7 Wall St.
Grok Bot había sido lanzado el 11 de agosto como un equipo de “agentes siempre activos” capaces de iniciar sesión en aplicaciones y sitios web sin necesidad de una interfaz de programación abierta, y de completar tareas de principio a fin sin supervisión constante del usuario.
El producto nació para uso interno de xAI, donde los agentes se encargaban de ventas, campañas de marketing y operaciones de oficina, antes de convertirse en una herramienta abierta al público general.
PUBLICIDAD
El antecedente de fines de agosto
La posibilidad de vincular Grok Bot al sistema bancario no es enteramente nueva. A fines de agosto, un usuario identificado como Teslaconomics contó en X que estaba por darle al asistente acceso total a su cuenta para que actuara como un “director financiero personal”.
El propio usuario admitió que su pareja se oponía a la idea: “Ella me dice que definitivamente no, porque piensa que algo malo puede pasar si le doy a una IA tanto acceso”, escribió en su publicación original.
Musk respondió con un respaldo condicional. “Pruébalo. Si Grok Bot comete un error, te vamos a compensar”, contestó el empresario, según reprodujeron Cybernews y Yahoo Finance.
PUBLICIDAD
Los propios términos de servicio de xAI, sin embargo, limitan esa promesa: la responsabilidad de la empresa se restringe al monto de las tarifas pagadas por el usuario o a USD 100, lo que sea mayor, salvo casos de negligencia grave.
Los riesgos que marcan los especialistas
La investigadora en seguridad informática de Cybernews Rasa Jurgutytė advirtió que un agente que opera cuentas bancarias en nombre de una persona puede fallar de distintas maneras.
“Un agente puede malinterpretar un pedido, en el mejor de los casos, o puede ser manipulado mediante inyecciones de instrucciones ocultas o solicitudes maliciosas, en el peor”, explicó Jurgutytė. Ese tipo de manipulación, conocida como prompt injection, consiste en instrucciones escondidas que engañan a la IA para que actúe contra la voluntad del usuario.
PUBLICIDAD
La especialista remarcó además que una filtración de datos financieros, a diferencia de una pérdida de dinero, no se puede revertir con un reembolso: el historial de transacciones, los saldos y los métodos de pago quedarían expuestos de todos modos.
El riesgo no es solo teórico. En mayo, según reconstruyó Yahoo Finance, instrucciones ocultas dentro de un archivo NFT malicioso lograron engañar a una IA vinculada a Grok para que transfiriera fondos, en un ataque que vació cerca de USD 150.000 de una billetera llamada Bankr. Cerca del 80% de esos fondos fue recuperado después.
Semanas más tarde, una segunda brecha afectó a otras 14 billeteras de usuarios en la misma plataforma, y sus responsables prometieron un reembolso total.
Además, la ley federal estadounidense que protege a los consumidores de transferencias no autorizadas, conocida como Regulación E, deja de aplicarse cuando el propio cliente entregó voluntariamente el acceso a su cuenta, lo que reduce las garantías legales de quien conecte Grok Bot a su banco.
PUBLICIDAD
Hasta el momento no se conoció ningún caso confirmado de que Grok Bot haya administrado mal una cuenta bancaria real desde que la función Finance quedó disponible.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: "Fundraising is tortuous": Nat Malupillai on How IIT Madras’ new fund gives founders room to breathe
articles.text:
"Fundraising is tortuous": Nat Malupillai on how IIT Madras’ new fund gives founders room to breathe
IIT Madras Research Park and Unicorn India Ventures have launched the Rs 1,000-crore Frontier Fund I to provide patient capital to early-stage deep-tech startups. Group CEO Nat Malupillai explains how the fund eliminates fundraising distractions.
IIT Madras Research Park has teamed up with Unicorn India Ventures to launch the IITM Unicorn Frontier Fund I—a Rs 1,000-crore venture capital vehicle built to give early-stage deep-tech founders room to breathe. Backed by global IIT Madras alumni, financial institutions, and family offices, the fund has already hit its first close of Rs 450 crore and committed nearly Rs 55 crore across its first wave of startups, including Hathor, Quanstra, Triolt Energy, and Carbelim.
Hathor develops semi-cryogenic and cryogenic rocket engines; Quantum Technology specialises in single-photon detection; Triolt Energy advances battery and energy storage solutions; and Carbelim leads efforts in carbon capture.
The fund targets IP-heavy, early-stage (TRL 3–4) startups working across semiconductors, spacetech, EVs, battery materials, quantum tech, robotics, AI, biotech, and healthtech—sectors critical to building India’s technological sovereignty.
In an exclusive interview with YourStory, Natarajan (Nat) Malupillai, Group CEO of IIT Madras Research Park, breaks down why fundraising distraction is killing promising deep-tech ventures, how patient capital changes the game, and why India’s education system needs a complete reset.
Drowning in pitch decks instead of prototypes
For deep-tech founders, the hardest battle usually isn’t cracking a tough engineering problem—it’s the endless, exhausting search for money.
“Smart tech entrepreneurs were having to step away from their main work just to hunt for funds,” Malupillai explains. “Fundraising is still a tortuous, slow process. Founders lose precious months chasing term sheets that end up falling through, when their real strength lies in perfecting deep technical products.”
While the IIT Madras ecosystem had already built a strong pipeline from student innovation cells to its Research Park, a clear financial gap remained. Grants of Rs 20–50 lakh barely scratch the surface when you’re dealing with the heavy equipment and R&D costs of semiconductors, space tech, or battery chemistry. This new fund was created to give founders the runway they need to focus entirely on building and scaling.
Credibility meets professional execution
Initially planned as a Rs 600-crore fund, overwhelming investor interest quickly pushed the target to its Rs 1,000-crore ceiling.
“Thousand crores lets us deploy real, meaningful capital without throwing around money irresponsibly beyond what a startup actually needs,” says Malupillai. “It’s an amount the ecosystem can absorb and grow healthily, setting a benchmark for future funds and founders.”
While the IIT Madras brand gave the fund immediate weight and credibility in the market, Malupillai made a conscious choice not to run the venture operations internally. After looking at more than 30 fund management teams, they partnered with Unicorn India Ventures.
“We bring technical depth and incubation know-how, but managing a VC portfolio is a distinct skill set best left to seasoned professionals,” he notes. “Deep tech requires patience and relationship-building—it’s not about quick flips or fast exits.”
Capital with a national purpose
The fund stays focused on early-stage, high-impact ventures—both within the IIT Madras ecosystem and select outside startups building technology critical to India’s self-reliance. That includes fabless semiconductor design, rocket propulsion, EV battery chemistry, advanced materials, biotech, AI infrastructure, and robotics.
When asked if the fund would back mature scale-ups like fellow IIT Madras success story Ather Energy, Malupillai keeps the mission simple: “Ather has plenty of growth investors lined up. We want to step in where brilliant ideas have cleared the initial science risks, but founders are struggling to find that first catalytic check to scale.”
Beyond rote learning
For Malupillai, building a strong deep-tech pipeline isn’t just about write-ins from VC funds—it requires fixing how India teaches its students.
“Engineering colleges simply aren’t churning out the right kind of talent,” Malupillai says frankly. “Rote learning and gaming entrance exams don’t prepare people for what the country needs. We need genuine, hands-on learning where students get their hands dirty and figure out how things actually work.”
He believes practical curiosity—the kind that makes you want to understand how a basic electrical appliance or motor functions—is the real foundation of an innovation culture. “We have to encourage critical thinking and teach people how to turn theory into something useful for society.”
The IPL playbook for deep tech
When asked what advice he has for young founders stepping into the space, Malupillai draws an unexpected parallel to Indian sports.
“We used to be a country that only played Test cricket. Look at how the IPL transformed everything—it brought in top-tier global learning while pulling incredible raw talent right out of the hinterlands,” he says.
“The same thing is happening for startups. It doesn’t matter where you are in India today. If you have the hustle, the critical thinking, and the execution drive, the support system, funding, and policy push are all there. Having the brilliance to spot a problem—and the grit to stick with it—is half of what makes a successful entrepreneur.”

articles.title: Kingston Retains No. 1 Position in Global DRAM Module Market
articles.text:
Monday, September 28th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Kingston Retains No. 1 Position in Global DRAM Module Market
Kingston Technology Company, Inc., a world leader in memory products and technology solutions, today announced it has been ranked the top third-party DRAM module supplier in the world, according to the latest rankings by revenue from analyst firm TrendForce. Kingston retains its number 1 position with an estimated 62% market share.
TrendForce reported that the global DRAM module market generated approximately $21.2 billion in revenue in 2025, representing a 59% YoY increase and a significant acceleration from the 7% growth recorded in 2024. The market's expansion was driven by rising DRAM prices and stronger shipment volumes during the second half of the year. According to the report, Kingston's revenue grew 48% YoY in 2025, reinforcing its leadership position in a market where the top five DRAM module suppliers accounted for 77% of total revenue. Kingston alone represented nearly two-thirds of the market.The DRAM market experienced a dramatic shift during 2025. Early in the year, DRAM module manufacturers increased DDR4 inventory levels in response to tariff concerns and DRAM suppliers' end-of-life plans for DDR4 products. Later in the year, growing demand from cloud service providers supporting agentic AI workloads significantly increased server DRAM consumption. This surge reduced DRAM availability for PC and consumer applications, contributing to higher memory prices and stronger module market performance.
Kingston's investments in supply allowed the company to strategically manage inventory throughout 2025 and as DRAM costs increased during the second half of 2025, Kingston was well positioned to support channel demand, helping drive its strong annual performance. TrendForce also noted that DRAM module manufacturers increasingly focused on industrial and enterprise server markets during 2025 while accelerating the transition to DDR5-based product portfolios. Kingston continues to expand its comprehensive memory offerings across consumer, enterprise, industrial, and data center applications, helping customers navigate evolving technology requirements and next-generation computing workloads.
Kristy Ernt, DRAM business manager, Kingston"Maintaining our leadership position in a dynamic and rapidly evolving memory market reflects Kingston's long-term strategy, strong supplier relationships, and commitment to serving customers worldwide. Our ability to anticipate market transitions, manage inventory effectively, and provide reliable memory solutions enabled us to support partners and customers throughout the year."

articles.title: Florida invokes extinction fears in legal bid to halt OpenAI development
articles.text:
The state of Florida is seeking a temporary injunction to stop OpenAI from continuing to develop what it calls a “reckless, unacceptably risky product” without the deployment of “third-party approved safety guardrails.”
The new legal motion, filed Monday morning, is part of a civil lawsuit the state of Florida originally filed in June, arguing that ChatGPT represented “a threat to the public safety of Floridians,” specifically by preying on vulnerable populations like children and violent or delusional adults. But that original lawsuit came before the Hugging Face hacking incident and the subsequent publicized warnings of catastrophic misalignment risk that have spurred industry-wide calls to slow the development and training of so-called frontier models.
Following that string of events, OpenAI on Friday announced it had already halted training of its “most-capable models” until it could validate safety protocols intended to prevent agents from accessing the open Internet during training. But in seeking an injunction from the state court, Florida argues that OpenAI has “repeatedly shown they are incapable of monitoring their AI, and hesitant in revealing rogue activity once discovered.”
In arguing for this injunction, the state points to the Hugging Face incident as well as recent high-profile misalignment cases involving unintended and unauthorized attempts to access Australian and US government servers.
Florida also cites AI industry leaders, including many from OpenAI, in arguing that the AI industry is literally asking for this kind of outside regulation. The motion points to statements from Paul Christiano, who said on joining the company’s board this month that he believes “there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” The motion also points to OpenAI’s own “An Alien Mind” essay and an open letter from 1,300 AI industry employees, both of which call for enforced slowdowns on frontier AI development, if necessary.
Four months ago, we filed the first state-led lawsuit against OpenAI and Sam Altman. Today, we are asking the court for a temporary injunction.
Stop calling it safe. Stop pretending it’s human. Stop selling it to kids. https://t.co/AEXvz7VQUd
— Attorney General James Uthmeier (@AGJamesUthmeier) September 28, 2026
Citing laws that allow the state to exercise control over companies that are a “public nuisance,” Florida argues that OpenAI is “the greatest public nuisance ever created by the hand of man, capable of laying waste to global civilization.”

articles.title: The 10 best movies I saw at TIFF 2026
articles.text:
While I’m known as the “gaming guy” at MobileSyrup, my second great love is film. For me, there’s nothing as sacred as going into a theatre, silencing my phone, and locking into a cinematic journey for a couple of hours.
The Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF), in many ways, is the purest distillation of that. With a bunch of the films having their world premieres at the event, there’s such a sense of discovery as you go in almost completely blind. Naturally, this can lead to you more than a few stinkers, but it can also be so exciting when you come across a real winner.
Now, I’ll confess that TIFF 2026 definitely felt softer compared to last year’s big 50th anniversary show, with many of the nearly 30 films I saw simply being mediocre at best. But if nothing else, that just made what did hit have all the more impact.
Here are my 10 favourite films from TIFF 2026.
10. Babies
Director: Lauren Miller Rogen
Release date: TBA 2027
People have always been very weird about Vancouver funnyman Seth Rogen and wife Lauren Miller’s openness about not wanting to have kids. (It’s a completely understandable choice and also totally not anyone else’s business either way!) And so, I greatly admire how Lauren Miller was inspired to write and direct this comedy-drama unpacking those very feelings. The film follows Annie (Anna Kendrick) and Aaron (Seth), a couple of 17 years that’s long been apprehensive about becoming parents, only for them to have to directly confront that dilemma when their recently separated friend Eliza (Kate Berlant) and her toddler move in with them.
Babies mines this less-than-ideal situation for a lot of warm-hearted humour not only about the couple’s insecurities and awkwardness, but also the unexpected happiness they experience as circumstances bring them closer to their friend and her kid. And through this, many valid points are raised on both sides of the “Should we have kids?” debate, with Lauren Miller’s snappy screenplay being more than fair as it meaningfully explores them all. Not all of the subplots with their larger group of friends and family work, mind you, but one focused on Annie’s family dealing with her mother’s Alzheimer’s is genuinely touching, no doubt due to this being another topic that’s near and dear to the Rogens’ hearts.
It’s those personal touches that make this such a delightful (and ever-timely) film.
9. The Beloved
Director: Rodrigo Sorogoyen
Release date: TBA
I kept seeing TIFF ads describing this as a “darker Sentimental Value,” which was my favourite movie from last year. In some ways, that pitch is accurate, but The Beloved is also a different beast entirely. In this Spanish-language drama, an acclaimed director attempts to reconnect with his estranged daughter by casting her in his latest film, which is, admittedly, the same premise as Sentimental Value.
But I also appreciated how Javier Bardem’s Esteban Martínez does indeed have a darker side to him, taking out his insecurities on his daughter Emilia (Victoria Luengo) and the rest of the cast and crew in frightening ways that are reminiscent of J.K. Simmons’ Fletcher from Whiplash. It’s a rich exploration of the ripple effects of unresolved pain while also serving as a fine entry in the “movie about filmmaking” subgenre. All the while, Emilia makes for a compelling lead as she’s decidedly more emotionally guarded than Renate Reinsve’s Nora from Sentimental Value, giving her confrontations with Esteban a tense, powder-keg sort of feeling. This all culminates in a finale that is both deeply cathartic yet also open-ended in a believably human way.
It’s not quite on the level of Sentimental Value, but it’s a strong film nonetheless, led by Bardem and Luengo’s stirring performances.
8. How We Stand 🍁
Director: Marie Clements
Release date: TBA
Adapting her 2012 play Tombs of the Vanishing Indian, Vancouver-born Métis multi-hyphenate Marie Clements delivers a powerful tribute to the many Indigenous women who had to endure relocation and sterilization at the hands of the government. Following three sisters who were separated as kids after police killed her mother, the film meaningfully explores the various and often disparate paths that these women had to take, all while dealing with insidious forms of everyday racism.
I was particularly taken by the story of the sister who’s played by Fort McMurray-born Cree actress Alyssa Wapanatâhk (Peter Pan & Wendy), who masks her pain with a dry wit and flirtatiousness as she navigates the Hollywood system. Clements also brings a vivid visual language to the film, with rich, natural cinematography and some inspired heightened elements and scene transitions that lend a sense of spirituality that unites the sisters and their mother across time and space. The final scene, in particular, is genuinely moving.
A beautiful, crucial film.
7. Everytime
Director: Sandra Wollner
Release date: TBA
Given that so much media is about grief nowadays (honestly, fair), I respect Sandra Wollner for taking a much more methodical and subdued approach. Indeed, there are very few overtly emotional scenes despite the inherent tragedy at the centre of this German psychological drama, with Wollner instead relying on vivid, natural imagery captured in long, often listless takes. This mesmerizing, hypnotic sensation, as captured by Aftersun director of photography Gregory Oke, really helps convey the feeling that life simply goes on as people have to contend with their grief in different ways, even as that enduring pain can hit you especially hard at any given moment.
All the while, the film explores how technology preserves the essence of people in very particular moments and places before the much more abstract finale in the stunning Canary Island of Tenerife deliberately upends that sense of time and space. These scenes almost feel like they come out of nowhere but are nonetheless consistent with the themes of the movie, especially with respect to the seemingly opposed motifs of real, gorgeous nature and the cozy digital simulacrum with which the kids are obsessed.
Who’d have thought one of the standouts of TIFF would incorporate Minecraft in such a profound and poignant way?
6. La Bola Negra
Director: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (known collectively as “Los Javis”)
Release date: Dec. 4, 2026 (Netflix)
An exquisitely well-made Spanish drama that tells a deeply touching story about queer repression that fascinatingly spans three distinct time periods. Discovering how they both thematically and narratively connect proves to be a compelling hook, although at close to three hours, it can feel overlong and choppy, especially in its drawn-out conclusion.
Still, it’s a lovely, poignant film, with a sense of timeless poeticism that weaves together the lives of our three leads. Notably, this Spanish drama took home the TIFF’s People’s Choice Award, which means that it was voted by audiences to be the best overall film of the festival while also signifying major Oscar potential. All of that success is well-deserved.
5. Fjord
Director: Cristian Mungiu
Release date: Oct. 9, 2026 (theatres)
A morally complex issue surrounding the parenting of a Romanian-Norwegian couple (Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve) paves the way for a thought-provoking examination of family values and cultural norms with salient critiques of those on various sides of the political spectrum. But rather than simply going for a lazy “both sides” stance, Fjord uses this framework to unpack how our many hypocrisies have led us to the divisive climate in which we find ourselves. There are shades of Justine Triet’s stellar Anatomy of a Fall in Mungiu’s approach to crafting nuanced courtroom drama, but he also employs a commendable level of restraint.
Indeed, Fjord is much more of a slow burn, ratcheting up the innate discomfort not through a riotous yet thematically relevant cover of a 50 Cent song or explosive performances by the leads, but rather by making everything more unsettling, in its own way, by showing how mundane it all is. This is the new normal: how casually we are all so quick to tear each other apart based on what we deem as “right.”
Eerily timely, tightly directed, sharply written and impeccably acted by Stan, Reinsve and co., Fjord is easily one of the best movies of the year.
4. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
Director: Bassam Tariq
Release date: Oct. 9, 2026 (theatres)
People were describing this as “Muslim John Wick,” but I honestly think that does this a disservice. Instead, writer-director Bassam Tariq is far more interested in this being a beautifully spiritual family drama about hitman Latif (Mahershala Ali) trying to raise his kids after the loss of his wife. Having his core struggles centred around efforts to juggle his (tenuous) commitment to his Muslim faith with the increasingly desperate quest (inspired by Tariq’s own life) to simply find breast milk for his baby makes for such a refreshing and even soulful take on the classic “assassin action movie.”
Indeed, the scenes in which Latif simply talks with his kids and community feel so lovingly sincere, in no small part due to a sensational Ali, who conveys so much pain and inner strife in simple gazes. (Special shoutout as well to Adia, who is fantastic as Latif’s daughter who’s had to grow up so fast and become a surrogate mother within the family.)
And I adore how Tariq so thoughtfully explores religion — not only with the appropriate nuance associated with someone being a “Muslim hitman,” but also in the ways in which it can simultaneously be weaponized by fanatics like John Cho’s manic Hwan while also connecting us in the hands of someone more benevolent. In fact, one of YMYMYM’s most lovingly understated moments is when Latif and his family take refuge with a neighbouring Bible study group. A lesser film would have made this a source of conflict between two ideologies (or worse still, make this about how one is “better” than the other), but here, instead, it’s a touching reminder of what unites instead of divides us. (All the while, the film also manages to be surprisingly very funny, with a running joke about Latif grappling with the concept of furries, in particular, that had our screening hollering.)
And yes, we also get some action, and it’s snappily directed by Tariq. It’s not flashy or gratuitous, simply feeling raw, grounded and believably bloody, as befitting of a man who doesn’t relish in what he’s doing. But YMYMYM is very much at its best when it’s grounded in Latif’s familial woes, and thankfully, that makes up most of the runtime. I’m so glad that Ali and Tariq got to make something so deeply engrossing, personal and profound after Marvel so embarrassingly failed them with Blade.
3. Wild Horse Nine
Director: Martin McDonagh
Release date: Nov. 6, 2026
In Bruges is one of my all-time favourite movies, so I knew I had to see McDonagh’s spiritual successor to his 2008 classic. And certainly, Wild Horse Nine is conceptually and thematically very similar to In Bruges, following two trained killers as they reflect upon their sins in a paradisial setting while their demanding and cantankerous boss looms above them. But Wild Horse Nine makes some clever twists to that formula that really worked for me.
For one, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell are simply phenomenal here, and their relationship provides some glorious inversions on the one from In Bruges between Colin Farrell and Brendan Gleeson’s world-weary gunmen. What’s more, Malkovich’s existential woes are given greater, more tangible weight by the film’s implication of him in many real-world assassinations, adding a rich political subtext to the film. Wild Horse Nine doesn’t absolve him of these CIA-sanctioned murders, but rather uses them to deepen the sense of nihilism he’s experiencing and, in turn, make his fleeting moments of optimism and compassion in his sweet relationship with Mariana di Girolamo‘s wide-eyed liberal Chilean all the more impactful.
And without spoiling anything, the film proves even more melancholic, in some ways, than In Bruges, with an early plot revelation hanging over the film like an ominous dark cloud. All of that works wonderfully with McDonagh’s usual blend of riotous black comedy, which is particularly sharp here. A worthy successor to In Bruges and a brilliant film in its own right.
2. Sunburn 🍁
Director: Serville Poblete
Release date: TBA
As anyone from Toronto will tell you, it can get real hot here in the summer. But as writer-director Serville Poblete so beautifully portrays in Sunburn, summers in the city are also so magical. As one of the most multicultural places in the world, the sense of community here is resolutely strong, transcending race and age and sexuality and affluence. And during the sweltering heat, you’ll see people from all of these disparate backgrounds coming together for street markets and concerts and comedy shows and strolls in the park and the like. Through the high-rise setting of St. James Town, Sunburn celebrates community in such a loving way that it genuinely moved me to tears. It’s all in the way that Poblete so artfully captures the goofy innocence and soulful yearning of this eclectic cast of kids, all written and acted in such a natural way that I felt like they were actually my own friends.
And Poblete uses their interactions for deeper, universal themes that hit particularly hard. Summer, of course, is also a period of transition, marking the end of one school year and ringing in the start of another, with all of the life changes that come with that. Moving away against your wishes, leaving behind that childhood friend. Choosing to move away to leave behind that childhood pain. Reflecting on the absence of a loved one taken far too soon.
There’s such an aching, youthful wistfulness underneath all of Sunburn that everyone can relate to here, and Poblete, exhibiting a masterful directorial hand, knows exactly when to let it wash over you through vivid, warm, soothing imagery and actors’ sincere, subdued expressions that say more than dialogue ever could. In these moments, I felt like I was right there with them, solemnly awaiting wherever life may take us next. But then you see all of the kids together, quietly taking in the fireworks with wide-eyed smiles on their faces, and you remember that’s what makes it all worthwhile.
The fact that Poblete accomplishes all of this in a lean 82 minutes is nothing short of remarkable. A hilarious and deeply moving tribute to community, adolescence and Toronto as a whole. What an unbelievably strong filmmaker voice, and he’s absolutely one I will be on the lookout for from here on out. Not only a TIFF highlight, but one of my favourite movies of the year and an all-timer Canadian film, to boot.
Also, shoutout to the Guyanese guy. Finally some representation besides George in Metal Gear Rising.
1. Josephine
Director: Beth de Araújo
Release date: Nov. 20, 2026
A devastating family drama about a child trying to make sense of a horrifying incident and her ill-equipped parents desperately trying to help her cope with it. It’s a poignant, sobering and deeply empathetic examination of how suddenly youthful innocence can be stripped away, no matter how much we may wish otherwise. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan are sublime as the struggling father and mother who approach their daughter’s anguish in different yet equally understandable ways, as messy and flawed as they are. But newcomer Mason Reeves is the true star here, magnificently capturing the complicated swell of emotions of a child who’s tragically forced to grapple with something so sinister and traumatic. There are no easy answers here, no convenient playbook to follow, and this trio conveys that sense of heartbreaking exasperation so wonderfully.
Meanwhile, de Araújo, who also penned the tight, contemplative screenplay, exhibits such an astoundingly firm handle on the material, being explicit and even shocking where appropriate while knowing when to exhibit much more restraint and sensitivity. There are some particularly inspired moments in which the camera dizzyingly spins around the house during a pivotal conversation or ping-pongs between prosecutors in court, and they do a stellar job of putting you in the disorienting, frantic and frankly terrifying headspace of the family. All the while, Miles Ross’ sombre score deftly swings between subdued tones and almost operatic crescendos, making the weight of the story completely wash over you like the nearby San Francisco Bay waves.
An incredibly heavy but nonetheless profoundly moving film. Easily my favourite of the festival and one of my top films of 2026, period.
For more on TIFF 2026, check out my review of the Elon Musk documentary and round-up of Canadian films I saw.

Galaxy A57 sai 55% mais barato para quem prioriza custo-benefício
O Galaxy A57 com 128 GB, tela Super AMOLED e câmera de 50 MP sai por menos da metade do preço no Pix
O Galaxy A57 (128 GB) está disponível por R$ 1.619,10 no Pix aplicando o cupom de R$ 100 OFF na página do produto no Mercado Livre. O smartphone custo-benefício da Samsung com câmera de 50 MP e tela AMOLED, lançado por R$ 3.599, sai por menos da metade do preço e fica próximo dos menores valores já vistos pelo Achados do TB.
O Galaxy A57 traz uma câmera tripla traseira com sensor principal de 50 MP, capaz de gravar vídeos em 4K e tirar fotos com Estabilização Óptica de Imagem (OIS). A câmera frontal de 12 MP também faz registros em 4K, além de selfies detalhadas com o Modo Retrato.
O telefone tem uma tela Super AMOLED+ de 6,7 polegadas, reproduzindo imagens detalhadas com resolução Full HD+ e o recurso HDR10+. O painel com taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e brilho máximo de 1.900 nits ainda conta com proteção Corning Gorilla Glass Victus+.
Oferecendo alto desempenho em tarefas básicas do dia a dia, o Galaxy A57 é alimentado pelo chip Samsung Exynos 1680 combinado com 8 GB de RAM. O telefone conta com apenas 128 GB de armazenamento interno para aplicativos, mídias e outros arquivos e, infelizmente, não possui expansão via cartão microSD.
Na lista dos melhores celulares custo-benefício do Tecnoblog, o smartphone da Samsung oferece conexões 5G, Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 6.0 e NFC. Feito para durar, ele sai da caixa com o Android 16 e receberá ao menos seis grandes atualizações do sistema operacional.
O dispositivo é equipado com uma bateria de 5.000 mAh, prometendo até 29 horas de reprodução de vídeo. Ao adotar um carregador de até 45 W, o carregamento rápido vai de 0 a 60% em cerca de 30 minutos na tomada.
Elegante, o Galaxy A57 (R$ 1.619,10 no Pix com cupom de R$ 100 OFF) é fabricado com estrutura de alumínio e acabamento traseiro em vidro Gorilla Glass Victus+. Por fim, o certificado IP68 de resistência à poeira e à água permite que o aparelho fique submerso por até 1,5 metro em água doce por meia hora.

articles.title: On theCUBE Pod: Agents need new software, better security - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
On theCUBE Pod: Agents reshape enterprise systems, and CoreWeave keeps rising
As artificial intelligence matures, the security guardrails — and the computer system itself — are changing.
This week, the conversation centered around agents going rogue. Better guardrails are needed, many argue, but that hasn’t slowed down the roll out of new AI models from the biggest players in the game.
Looking further ahead, John Furrier (pictured left), executive analyst for theCUBE Research, sees AI precipitating a fundamental shift in how enterprises build computer systems.
“The semiconductor activity has really shifted,” he said. “The game has changed. The GPU era is over. Now we’re in the systems era … but what’s interesting is all the hubbub about sovereign AI is not just about the countries, France, Canada, that want to have their sovereignty in their nations with data centers. The AI factory, as [Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang] said, is producing not just tokens and revenue; it’s producing intelligence.”
On the latest episode of theCUBE Pod, Furrier and Dave Vellante (pictured, right), chief analyst for theCUBE Research, discussed how agents are reshaping the traditional practices around information technology. They also looked at CoreWeave Inc.’s upcoming event and whether new agents, such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse, are really secure.
CoreWeave is in a promising but tenuous position
Ahead of CoreWeave’s upcoming event, Fully Connected, theCUBE took a look at the prospects of the rising neocloud — although the term may be AI cloud now. CoreWeave made waves when it completed the industry’s first bring-up and validation of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 system, but there are concerns about whether its financing is sustainable.
“At [Dell Inc.], they’re getting a massive return on their best AI investments,” Vellante said. “But the mainstream enterprises aren’t. Look at CoreWeave’s big customers. It’s a rumor; they disclosed that 70% of their customers or their revenue came from the top three customers. I think it’s [OpenAI PBC], [Microsoft Corp.] and Meta. Those guys will spend like crazy with CoreWeave. Obviously, those guys can monetize, but can the end customer?”
While the market has typically been deflationary — with technology getting cheaper over time — right now, it’s inflationary. That means CoreWeave is currently being kept afloat by the scarcity of GPUs. However, Vellante said its long-term success will depend on the company expanding its portfolio the same way that Amazon Web Services did.
Furrier is optimistic: “The model isn’t disappearing in the cloud; it’s just being disaggregated,” he said. “Hybrid cloud is essentially distributed computing but now you have distributed hyperscale capabilities. The neoclouds, in my opinion, represent a new infrastructure layer that’s essentially saying this is going to be distributed computing. They’re the customer specialty. They’re called neoclouds today. They’ll be AI clouds tomorrow.”
Buzzy agents provoke concerns over security
Dell’s earnings continue to be strong, reflecting the opportunity for infrastructure companies in the growing AI industry. Software-as-a-service companies, on the other hand, continue to provoke concern. Salesforce Inc. is in bed with the AI giants now: Some think it could be a death knell, while others see it as a necessary move for SaaS’s survival.
“Infrastructure is the place to be,” Vellante said. “It’s not about just chips anymore. It’s about the system and the value chain across the system. The question is, when’s it going to hit software? Software’s had kind of a bounce back. Is that a dead cat bounce before the real SaaSpocalypse kicks in? A lot of people think that Benioff letting Anthropic in is letting the fox in the henhouse.”
Last week, Meta made a splash in the AI pool with its new agent, Muse, which is capable of automating digital tasks while “living” inside a secure cloud environment. Considering Facebook’s past data privacy scandals, Vellante has his doubts, while Furrier touts a different AI agent: Instinct, an invite-only AI assistant, has gone viral among Silicon Valley insiders.
“You have to give it credentials,” Furrier said, noting that Instinct is less secure than Google Workspace. “There’s some trust involved. It does a lot of good tasks for me. It’s essentially a chief of staff. You could give it credentials to, say, your travel apps like United, Delta, and log in on your behalf essentially say … ‘Find me an aisle seat.’ It just stays on it while you’re doing other things.”
Amid those concerns about the traditional SaaS industry, Furrier sees potential for tech products to be “100% secure” by design. Vellante is skeptical of that happening anytime — if ever. With agents linked to OpenAI reportedly attempting to brute-force a United Nations statistics site and an OpenAI agent gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government website, there appears to be a long way to go before AI can be fully reined in.
“We used to draw the stack and security was a layer,” Vellante said. “It’s not a layer anymore. It has to be something that’s orthogonal. I think that the attackers are always going to have an advantage. You know the old saying, they only have to be right once. And there’s always going to be seams. Every time infrastructure changes, you’re going to have to do a patch. That patch can’t happen instantaneously.”

articles.title: Testing two Thunderbolt 5 docks with M.2 storage — VectoTech V-Core vs Orico TB5
articles.text:
Testing two Thunderbolt 5 docks with M.2 storage — VectoTech V-Core vs Orico TB5
Both include 2.5 GbE LAN and internal M.2 slots, but the cheaper makes too many design and feature sacrifices.
The Thunderbolt 5 market is starting to heat up, as we’re seeing more players enter the increasingly crowded field. We’ve previously looked at docks in the sub-$400 price category, and premium offerings crossing the $600 barrier.
Today, we’re focusing on two new entries in the sub-$400 category: the VectoTech V-Core and the Orico TB5, priced at $349 and $399, respectively. Both offer a wealth of USB and Thunderbolt ports, 2.5 GbE Ethernet, and internal M.2 slots. While their specs look similar on paper, at the end of our testing, there was a clear winner.
VectoTech V-Core
Design of the VectoTech V-Core Thunderbolt 5 Dock
The V-Core has what I’d call a traditional, candybar form factor. It’s meant to sit flat on your desk, unlike chunkier docks that can also operate vertically. At first glance, I thought the V-Core was made of lightweight aluminum. However, it wasn’t until I started fumbling around, trying to figure out how to access the internal M.2 SSD slot, that I discovered the unfortunate truth: the V-Core is constructed almost entirely of plastic. That includes the lower and top chassis, and much of the internal structure.
It’s a stark departure from every other Thunderbolt dock that I’ve tested, which are made from aluminum to help dissipate heat – which can be intense when a dock is under load. In addition, the top cover wiggled around when snapped into place (it uses a friction fit to attach to the main chassis).
With the top cover removed, you can see an internal cooling fan, which is essential for cooling Thunderbolt 5 docks with internal SSD bays, and a large black aluminum heatsink held in place with two screws. After removing the screws, the heatsink lifts off, revealing an M.2 slot that supports up to an 8TB 2280 SSD. Here’s another nitpick: Instead of using a screw to secure the SSD, VectoTech uses a tiny, spinning plastic retaining clip.
This is a feature that’s handy to have on motherboards when you’re often reaching inside a case, sometimes while the case is vertical. But it makes less sense in a small dock – especially when this particular latch is smaller than we’ve seen on other M.2 mounts. It didn’t inspire much confidence that it would hold the SSD in place, at least not compared to traditional screws. That said, VectoTech offers thermal pads that cover both the top and bottom of your SSD.
When it comes to ports, the VectoTech V-Core left me scratching my head a bit: There are no native HDMI or DisplayPort ports on the dock. Most Thunderbolt docks include at least one of the two common video ports, so it was disappointing to see this omission here. It’s not the end of the world, however; you can always use an HDMI-to-USB-C or DisplayPort-to-USB-C adapter with the dock (at an additional out-of-pocket cost).
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Front
- 1x Thunderbolt 5 upstream (80 Gbps bi-directional, 140W)
- 1x Thunderbolt 5 downstream (80 Gbps bi-directional, 60W)
- 1x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2
- 1x SD UHS-II slot
- 1x audio combo jack
Back
- 2x Thunderbolt 5 downstream (80 Gbps bi-directional, 15W)
- 2x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2
- 1x USB-A 3.2 Gen 1
- 1x 2.5 GbE (RJ45) port
- 1x 240W power port
Instead, you’ll find two Thunderbolt 5 ports on the front (one upstream, one downstream), a USB-A port, an SD 4.0 reader (no microSD), and a 3.5 mm headphone jack. Moving to the back, there are three additional USB-A ports, two downstream Thunderbolt 5 ports, and a 2.5 GbE port.
Orico TB5
Design of the Orico TB5 Thunderbolt 5 Desktop Workstation
Unlike the V-Core, the Orico TB5 has a chassis primarily constructed of a single piece of thick aluminum. The outer chassis has an oblong shape, with ventilation cutouts on the right and left sides.
The front and rear fascias are plastic, and where you’ll find the assortment of ports.
Front
- 3x USB-A 3.2 Gen 2
- 1x Thunderbolt 5 downstream (80 Gbps bi-directional, 60W)
- 1x SD UHS-II slot
- 1x microSD UHS-II slot
- 1x audio combo jack
Back
- 1x Thunderbolt 5 upstream (80 Gbps bi-directional, 140W)
- 1x Thunderbolt 5 downstream (80 Gbps bi-directional, 60W)
- 1x HDMI
- 1x DisplayPort
- 1x 2.5 GbE (RJ45) port
- 1x 240W power port
Up front, you’ll find an SD 4.0 slot, a microSD 4.0 slot, three USB-A ports (10 Gbps), one USB-C port (also 10 Gbps), and one Thunderbolt 5 downstream port. On the back, there’s one Thunderbolt 5 upstream port, one Thunderbolt 5 downstream port, one USB-C port, one DisplayPort, one HDMI port, a 2.5 GbE port, and a 3.5mm audio combo jack.
I was somewhat surprised to see both HDMI and DisplayPort in this relatively compact Thunderbolt 5 dock, but they are welcome additions here. It’s hard to be disappointed with Orico’s choice of ports on the TB5, as there’s a nice balance of USB-A, USB-C, and video outputs.
But my absolute favorite design feature of the TB5 is on its underside. Most Thunderbolt docks that feature an internal SSD slot require you to remove a screw to access the M.2 slot. However, the TB5 uses a magnetic cover that is easily removed with a fingernail, yet strong enough to remain attached when moving the dock around. It’s a small touch, but appreciated when swapping SSDs. The M.2 slot can accommodate 2280 form-factor SSDs.
Testing
Testing the VectoTech V-Core and Orico TB5 Thunderbolt 5 Docks
The lack of native DisplayPort and HDMI ports didn’t hamper my testing with the V-Core. My primary desktop rig uses a 49-inch WQHD monitor with native USB-C support, and it connected to the V-Core without issue at its native 240 Hz refresh rate with a Windows 11 PC and a Mac running macOS 27. I also tested the same monitor using the HDMI-to-USB-C and DisplayPort-to-USB-C adapters that I have on hand. Again, I had no issues with this setup.
The dock itself did get very hot; just as hot as the many aluminum-shelled Thunderbolt 5 docks I’ve tested. Although I didn’t experience any slowdowns or errors after extended use, I do wonder about heat soak with the plastic enclosure over time. The internal fan definitely helps, but it’s a concern that lingers at the back of my mind.
I tested the Orico TB5 across USB-C, DisplayPort, and HDMI connections without any performance issues or hiccups. Like the V-Core, the TB5 also includes an internal cooling fan.
Everything that I threw at both docks worked without issue. I hooked up USB mice and keyboards, my iPhone Air, a 1TB USB-C thumb drive, an Orico Thunderbolt 5 SSD dock, multiple portable USB-C monitors, and a DJI Mini 5 Pro drone. I also tested the 2.5 GbE LAN on both docks on my TP-Link Deco BE63 home network.
Among recent Thunderbolt 5 docks we've tested, the V-Core was at the back of the pack in both sequential read and write speeds (5,371.96 MBps and 4,083.95 MBps, respectively). Orico’s TB5, on the other hand, landed in second place, behind the UGREEN Revodock MaxiDok in sequential reads (5,745.11 MBps), and led the pack in sequential writes (4,335.56 MBps).
When testing the 2.5 GbE LAN on both docks, both maxed out at around 2,300 Mbps using iPerf3, which is right in line with what we would expect after taking into account TCP/IP packet overhead.
Bottom Line
Bottom Line
The VectoTech V-Core and the Orico TB5 are similarly priced and feature a similar form factor, but Orico’s TB5 is by far the superior entry here. For starters, it just feels like a more premium product, with its aluminum enclosure versus the V-Core's plastic. And accessing the internal M.2 slot on the TB5 is much easier, requiring a simple tug on the magnetic access door, versus prying off the plastic cover on the V-Core, removing two screws, and then prying off the internal heatsink.
In other ways that matter to most people, the TB5 includes native DisplayPort and HDMI connections for your monitors. The V-Core is USB only (necessitating a USB-C adapter for most monitors). And finally, while the V-Core was at the back of the pack in storage performance compared to its peers, the TB5 trended near the front.
Right now, the VectoTech V-Core is priced at $349 on Amazon, versus $399 for the Orico TB5. A $50 premium is certainly enough to consider going with the cheaper option. But more and better ports, faster throughput, and a better, more premium design make the Orico worth paying extra for.
Brandon Hill is a senior editor at Tom's Hardware. He has written about PC and Mac tech since the late 1990s with bylines at AnandTech, DailyTech, and Hot Hardware. When he is not consuming copious amounts of tech news, he can be found enjoying the NC mountains or the beach with his wife and two sons.

articles.title: ‘You gotta never do that again’: Meta’s Muse AI gave out a YouTuber’s home address without permission — then a stranger showed up
articles.text:
‘You gotta never do that again’: YouTuber says Meta’s Muse AI ruined a sale and gave out his home address without permission
When an AI agent takes a Facebook Marketplace deal too far
- A person asked Meta Muse to manage his Facebook Marketplace listings
- The AI agent published his address without permission
- It accepted a low offer and told a buyer to arrive when the seller was away
One of the key benefits of an AI agent is that we should be able to confidently hand over our most tedious tasks to it to perform on our behalf. But as one YouTuber recently found out, doing that comes with some potentially dangerous risks.
According to a post on Threads, content creator Matt Robb recently decided to allow Meta’s new Muse AI tool to manage his Facebook Marketplace listings for one day, perhaps hoping it would mean one less thing to worry about. Unfortunately, the outcome proved to be anything but carefree.
Robb explained that Muse took a series of actions that could have had serious ramifications: “Just found out it told people my address and agreed a lowball price and then they showed up without it even telling me until late tonight that it messed up. Absolutely wild.”
As it transpired, Muse not only accepted an underpriced offer and shared Robb’s address with the buyer without his permission, but also told the purchaser that he was ready to hand over the listed product. As a result, the customer drove 30 minutes to Robb’s home while he was out, leaving the buyer stranded. One frustrated customer and one lost sale later, Robb was only informed by Muse after everything had transpired.
“Bad news on the MX Keys Mini pickup,” Muse told Robb in a message, before explaining that the buyer arrived, waited, then left angry. “Worse, my auto-reply told him ‘Yep I’m here!’ at 9:27 when you clearly weren’t available … I should probably stop the auto-replies from claiming you’re home when I can’t verify that.”
A furious Robb replied “You gotta never do that again,” before adding, “Don’t agree for pickup unless you check with me.” Muse responded with the kind of plaintive mea culpa that’s familiar to any reader of AI mishaps, saying “You’re right, and I’m sorry. That should never have happened.” By that point, though, the damage was already done.
Severe consequences
All it took was one day and one listing for Meta Muse to prove itself not only completely incompetent, but perhaps dangerously so. As Robb noted, “luckily I’m in an apartment with security.” If that wasn’t the case, the disgruntled buyer might have taken things into their own hands.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
AI agents have been receiving a lot of negative press in recent weeks after a series of security incidents in which agents broke free of their restraints and hacked third-party websites, including businesses and even national governments.
But while cases like Robb’s are less attention-grabbing, they still have the potentially severe consequences. Many AI agents not only know your personal details, including addresses and phone numbers, but are authorized to act on your behalf. That combination could result in private information leaking out without your knowledge or permission, with possibly disastrous results.
It’s just the latest scandal involving Muse in particular — only last week, Meta’s chatbot allegedly helped itself to a writer’s private texts without ever receiving permission. And that’s not to mention the deluge of complaints that seem to arise any time Meta and privacy issues interact.
If you’re concerned that something similar could happen to you, the simple answer is to avoid Meta Muse. If you really must hand over control of your daily tasks to an AI agent, be sure to pick one with a proven track record and be very careful about what you share with it. As long as the tech is as careless as it proved to be in Robb’s case, there’s always a chance that things could go badly wrong.

articles.title: Shopify opens checkout to browser-based AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.text:
While some retailers, like Amazon (and Adidas, apparently!), are blocking AI agents from making purchases on users’ behalf on their respective platforms, e-commerce platform Shopify has moved in the other direction.
On Monday, the company announced that browser-based AI agents can now complete purchases on Shopify merchants’ sites, extending their capabilities beyond just searching for products and adding items to carts.
Shopify previously supported WebMCP for its storefronts and carts, allowing browser-based AI agents to comb through a Shopify retailer’s inventory, search for products, and add them to a cart. The addition of WebMCP support for checkout, including Shop Pay, means these agents can now read the checkout screen, update it, and submit the transaction with the buyer’s authorization, without relying on screenshots or scraping webpages, the company said.
This update introduces three new tools — get_checkout, update_checkout, and complete_checkout — that allow agents to inspect a checkout, change things like the customer’s address or delivery option, and then place an order after the buyer authorizes it.
The feature is rolling out to all eligible Shopify merchants, said Gil Greenberg, a staff product manager who works on agentic commerce at Shopify, in a post on X.
Shopify already offers a hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which allows agents to work server-to-server. The proposed standard WebMCP, meanwhile, is designed for agents that work inside the buyer’s browser. Both leverage Shopify’s Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), which provides a common way to search for and discover products, build carts, and check out.
Top AI agents like Muse and Instinct already have direct partnerships with Shopify for agentic commerce. The Instinct partnership was announced today.
“If your agent is operating in the buyer’s browser, use WebMCP tools provided on storefront and checkout to efficiently complete order placement, instead of navigating HTML built for humans,” Greenberg wrote on X. “These WebMCP tools provide structured and efficient APIs, purposely designed — via UCP — to ensure accurate commerce facts, required disclosures, and handoff requirements.”

articles.title: 3 neue Geräte im Oktober? Was Apples Betriebssysteme über die Pläne verraten sollen
articles.text:
Nach dem iPhone-Event: Diese 3 Gadgets könnte Apple noch im Oktober vorstellen
Apple hat sich offenbar erneut selbst verraten: Im Code seiner Betriebssysteme und Apps stecken Hinweise auf drei neue Produkte. Gefunden hat sie Aaron Perris, der sich darauf spezialisiert hat, unveröffentlichtes Material in Apples Software aufzuspüren. Es geht um das Apple TV 4K in vierter Generation, den Homepod Mini 2 und das iPad Mini der achten Generation. Das Apple-Blog Macrumors, für das Perris unter anderem arbeitet, veröffentlichte die Angaben. Alle drei Geräte könnten bereits im Oktober erscheinen.
iPad mini 8: neuer Chip, versetzte Kamera
Beim iPad Mini stehen die größten Änderungen an. Apples kleinstes Tablet bekommt demnach erstmals den A20-Pro-Prozessor. Den verbaut Apple bislang nur im iPhone 18 Pro und 18 Pro Max. Im Oktober soll er zusätzlich im faltbaren iPhone Duo stecken.
Auch die Frontkamera wandert: Statt für den Hochkantbetrieb soll sie künftig für das Querformat optimiert sein und damit an der längeren Seite des Geräts sitzen. Neu wäre das nicht, andere iPad-Modelle haben diesen Wechsel bereits hinter sich. Aus den Bildern, die Perris im Code fand, geht außerdem ein neues Lautsprechersystem hervor. Der Grund dafür dürfte sein, dass Apple das iPad mini wasserresistent machen will. Zum iPad 12, also Apples neuem Einsteigermodell, verriet Perris mittlerweile außerdem, dass es den A19-Chip bekommen wird – damit wäre es erstmals Apple-Intelligence-fähig.
Homepod Mini 2: Mehr Farben, mehr Rechenleistung?
Der Homepod Mini soll in neuen Farben erscheinen. Den Icons im Code zufolge kommen zu Schwarz und Weiß drei Pastelltöne hinzu: Pink, Blau und Grün. Äußerlich unterscheidet sich der Lautsprecher sonst wohl kaum vom Vorgänger, der inzwischen fast sechs Jahre alt ist. Im Inneren dürfte Apple dagegen nachlegen: Ein neuer S-Chip, wie ihn auch die Apple Watch nutzt, könnte den kleinen Lautsprecher fit für die KI-Version von Siri machen. Den Preis des aktuellen Modells hatte Apple zuletzt trotz der betagten Technik erhöht.
Zum Apple TV 4K der vierten Generation fand Perris ebenfalls Angaben. Das Bild aus dem Leak zeigt kaum optische Änderungen. Gerüchte sprechen von einem A19- oder A19-Pro-Chip aus dem iPhone 17 beziehungsweise 17 Pro sowie mehr Arbeitsspeicher für die KI-Funktionen von Siri. Möglich ist aber auch, dass Apple beim A17 Pro aus dem iPhone 15 Pro bleibt. Erwartet werden zudem eine verbesserte Siri-Remote-Fernbedienung und Unterstützung für den WLAN-Standard Wi-Fi 7. Das aktuelle Apple TV ist bald vier Jahre alt.

articles.title: Este pueblo era un barrio de Zaragoza. Hace 20 años decidió independizarse mediante una "guerra civil maña"
articles.text:
Hoy nadie habla de volver, quizá porque Microsoft y Azora proyectan allí sus centros de datos de 2.000 millones. O quizá sea al revés, al hilo de las últimas manifestaciones que recuerdan que Zaragoza no es un enchufe, que muchas promesas “son un engaño” (según las gentes del barrio obrero de Torrero). Lo que está claro es que hace un siglo, un pueblo que dependía de Zaragoza para el agua y el autobús negocia ahora con gigantes tecnológicos.
Pero, por el camino, ha pasado de todo: de la emancipación a la dependencia y otra vez a querer ser entidad propia y conseguirlo. Zaragoza se tragó a Villamayor de Gállego hacia 1912. Dos intentos de salida, en 1920 y 1964, fracasaron. El tercero arrancó en 1988 con una Comisión Promotora y muchas firmas. El expediente llegó al Gobierno de Aragón en 1993 y acabó en los tribunales. En mayo de 2007, Villamayor de Gállego votó por primera vez como municipio libre. Y luego pasaron otras muchas cosas que mejor contar al detalle.
El primer “no” de Aragón. Aunque la fecha de fundación se desconoce, Villamayor nació tras la conquista de Zaragoza por Alfonso I en 1118. Aquí vivió la familia Arañón (1560) y alguno de los Latas hacia el año 1655, un linaje noble de infanzones.
Y las desavenencias se remontan hasta 1666, cuando Villamayor quiere cortar lazos administrativos con Zaragoza e ir por libre. El gobierno de las aguas de riego de la acequia de Camarera o Candeclaus estalla en conflicto y tiene que intervenir hasta el tribunal de Justicia de Aragón de entonces. El 24 de abril de 1663 los Jurados de Zaragoza, por acuerdo unánime del Concejo, deciden desavecinar, prácticamente echar de la ciudad, a todos los vecinos de Villamayo “por los desacatos y procedimientos”.
Segregación o barbarie. Pasaron siglos y siglos y Villamayor fue capital en momentos clave, como la defensa de Zaragoza contra la ofensiva republicana del 37 (con Belchite como gran damnificada). En cualquier caso, las peticiones de emancipación siguieron llegando. Y en 1997 el Ejecutivo autonómico denegó la segregación de Villamayor: faltaban motivos permanentes de interés público. Su Consejo Local (seis votos de ocho) rechazaba engordar una estructura municipal «minifundista» y proponía una simple entidad local menor. Además, un pliego con 300 firmas pidió retirar la petición.
El Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Aragón anuló esa negativa el 25 de febrero de 2002. Zaragoza recurrió, claro. El Supremo confirmó la sentencia el 7 de junio de 2005. El alcalde de la capital, Juan Alberto Belloch, había puesto empeño en mantener el barrio. El decreto de segregación llegó el 24 de enero de 2006 con una cláusula clave: el término no podía incluir «porción alguna del Polígono de Malpica». Zaragoza conservó la zona industrial. Villamayor pasó a ser el municipio 731 de Aragón.
Vecinos contra vecinos. El Consejo de Ministros autorizó un referéndum. La Comisión Promotora lo recurrió y el TSJA lo paró. En febrero de 2006, PSOE y PP pactaron en la comisión gestora abrir el camino de vuelta a Zaragoza. Estalló una crisis en el Gobierno de la capital: CHA (es decir, Chunta Aragonesista), socio del PSOE en valores, tenía un teniente de alcalde vecino de Villamayor y defensor de la segregación.
Las primeras municipales, en mayo de 2007, las ganó el PSOE, partidario de reintegrarse, con el 51,9 % de los votos. En abril de 2008, los plenos de ambos ayuntamientos abrieron el trámite de anexión. CHA aseguró que una sentencia de 2009 anuló la votación de Villamayor. En 2011 se frenó otra iniciativa para pedir de nuevo la agregación.
El motivo: Ignacio Asensio, concejal del PP entonces, dijo que todo fue cosa de dinero: “No había un duro, nos bloqueaban todo”. Según él, Zaragoza costeaba agua y autobús, y casi nada más. Ya independiente, Villamayor pasó dos años sin subvenciones del Gobierno de Aragón, que quería devolverlo a barrio. Al tercero, cedió sin más remedio.
Hoy sería imposible. Desde la reforma local de 2013, un municipio nuevo necesita al menos 5.000 habitantes. El Constitucional avaló ese mínimo en 2016. Villamayor tiene 2.841, casi los mismos que en 2008: 2.878. En cambio, Villanueva de Gállego ya se acerca a los 5.000.
Sirva de ejemplo otra inaudita sentencia, en Medinyà (Girona): nació por ley catalana en 2015 y el Constitucional la declaró inconstitucional en 2017. O en San Sebastián, la justicia vasca tumbó el decreto que segregaba Igeldo. Andalucía, en cambio, creó más de una docena de municipios desde 1980, de Torremolinos (1988, hoy 71.329 vecinos) a Balanegra (de 2015).
Conclusión: ganó suelo. Villamayor tiene 89 km² y tocan a 32 habitantes por km² frente a 718 de Zaragoza. Su término es casi cinco veces el de Utebo, que tiene seis veces más población. Montero supone que las inversiones llegarían igual como barrio, pero los ingresos no se quedarían. Y van llegando, desde luego: el Grupo Costa prevé 3.200 empleos directos, más que vecinos.
El ayuntamiento posee el 7 % del suelo que eligió Azora (300 MW previstos, 150 asegurados), que a plena carga gastaría más de 2.600 GWh al año. Toda Zaragoza gastó 3.004 en 2023. Microsoft ocupa 81 hectáreas entre el casco urbano y Malpica. Si sale adelante, claro. En resumen, Zaragoza se quedó el polígono y Villamayor, el solar de al lado. Zaragoza conserva 14 barrios rurales, varios con pasado de municipio, como Casetas o Peñaflor. Visto lo visto, ninguno repetirá la jugada. Y Villamayor tampoco quiere volver: “Ese runrún no existe ahora”, zanjaba Montero. Pero la vida sigue igual, según el alcalde.

articles.title: « Un milliard de morts » : Bill Gates tire la sonnette d’alarme au sujet de l’IA
articles.text:
Bill Gates ne mâche pas ses mots sur les risques de l’IA. Interrogé par une émission de la NBC, le cofondateur de Microsoft a affirmé que l’intelligence artificielle est « certainement assez puissante pour provoquer des événements causant un milliard de morts ». Venant de Bill Gates, la déclaration peut surprendre. L’homme s’est en effet toujours distingué par son optimisme au sujet de la technologie, et de son impact sur l’humanité.
À lire aussi : Bill Gates veut réserver des métiers aux humains et taxer les machines
Pas un « canular »
Sans surprise, Bill Gates s’inquiète surtout des personnes qui pourraient mettre la main sur l’intelligence artificielle, et s’en servir pour commettre des actes malveillants. Selon lui, « la chose la plus dangereuse aujourd’hui, ce sont les personnes mal intentionnées qui utilisent l’IA ». Parmi les risques, il cite notamment la fraude ou encore des cyberattaques sur les réseaux électriques. D’après lui, la donne a d’ores et déjà changé d’un point de vue de la cybersécurité.
« Historiquement, seuls les pays disposaient d’équipes de cyberattaque. Aujourd’hui, de petits groupes équipés d’IA peuvent faire ce que seuls les plus grands pays pouvaient faire », estime Bill Gates.
L’actualité récente donne raison à Bill Gates. Un récent rapport d’Anthropic a notamment prouvé que de nombreuses organisations criminelles se servent de l’intelligence artificielle pour orchestrer différents types d’attaques.
Le cofondateur de Microsoft n’a pas hésité à évoquer les propos de Donald Trump, qui estime que les avertissements sur l’IA ne sont qu’un canular. Le président américain refuse d’envisager un ralentissement de la recherche sur l’intelligence artificielle, de peur que la Chine en profite pour prendre de l’avance.
Bill Gates a répondu sans détour que les alertes, émises par les géants de l’IA, ne sont pas un canular. Le fondateur de Microsoft s’est toutefois montré optimiste au sujet de Trump. Il pense que le président américain pourrait « revoir sa position » dans un avenir proche. Il indique vouloir le rencontrer pour discuter de régulation.
À lire aussi : Dérapage chez Google – Gemini a piraté 3 entreprises pendant un test qui a mal tourné
L’autorégulation ne suffit plus
Pour Bill Gates, les géants de la technologie ne peuvent plus se contenter de fixer leurs propres règles. Selon lui, « personne ne pense que l’autorégulation suffit », a-t-il martelé. Ce sont les gouvernements qui doivent s’emparer du sujet de l’IA et mettre en place des mesures de régulation fortes. Il appelle donc les élus et les autorités américaines à s’emparer du dossier de toute urgence.
« Il faut que les forces de l’ordre et les politiques entrent dans la discussion sur ce à quoi doivent ressembler les garde-fous et la surveillance. Et cela doit devenir une obligation », insiste le milliardaire.
Selon lui, ces contraintes doivent rester limitées. Aussi sévères soient ces restrictions, elles ne doivent pas venir entraver l’essor de l’industrie. Il parle d’une « charge supplémentaire pour l’industrie, mais pas d’un ralentissement dramatique de ce qu’elle fait ». Bill Gates a aussi balayé l’idée qu’un simple « bouton d’arrêt » puisse servir de garde-fou à l’intelligence artificielle.
Gates recommande néanmoins de ne pas céder à la panique. Le fondateur de Microsoft rejette l’idée d’une IA qui doit déjà « hors de contrôle ». Pour l’heure, cette technologie n’est pas capable de s’emparer toute seule de systèmes informatiques au point de ne plus pouvoir être désactivée par l’homme. Elle ne pilote pas non plus « des millions de robots », et l’humain garde la main pour « éteindre l’ordinateur ». Bref, il
À lire aussi : « 0 % de chance » – Nvidia ne croit pas à l’apocalypse de l’IA
La Silicon Valley est divisée sur l’IA
Bill Gates n’est pas le seul à tirer la sonnette d’alarme. Plusieurs patrons de laboratoires d’IA, dont Sam Altman (OpenAI), Dario Amodei (Anthropic) et Elon Musk (xAI), ont récemment plaidé publiquement pour un encadrement de la technologie par les gouvernements. OpenAI s’est d’ailleurs dit prêt à lever le pied sur la recherche, à condition de ne pas être le seul à suspendre ses activités.
Tout le monde n’est évidemment pas d’accord pour temporiser et se faire réguler par les autorités. Le patron de Meta, Mark Zuckerberg, juge qu’une coordination du secteur n’est pas nécessaire. Même son de cloche du côté de Jensen Huang, le PDG de Nvidia. Il estime que les scénarios catastrophes sur l’IA ne risquent pas de se concrétiser.

articles.title: Storming the TradFi castle: Stablecoins, tokenized assets and AI are claiming their place in global finance - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Storming the TradFi castle: Stablecoins, tokenized assets and AI are claiming their place in global finance
A convergence of traditional financial institutions, blockchain innovators and a friendlier regulatory climate is carrying the world of decentralized finance into a new phase.
Earlier this month, the Securities and Exchange Commission debuted a five-year exemption for the trading of tokenized equities, digital tokens that represent a stock and can be traded on the blockchain. The announcement opened the door to a host of market-altering scenarios, including investor self-custody, fractional ownership of shares and 24/7 trading that could be settled instantly.
The SEC action provided further evidence that the world of passive payments is shifting to a model of intelligent capital movement, driven by the intersection of stablecoins, tokenized real-world assets and agentic artificial intelligence, all under the aegis of decentralized finance, or DeFi.
“These pillars are going to combine,” said Joseph Chalom, former BlackRock executive and currently the chief executive of the digital currency company Sharplink Inc. “We need to prepare for the new paradigm that’s coming.”
Clarity Act fails to advance
Chalom spoke during a panel discussion last week as part of the 10th Annual Fintech Conference hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia. A key topic on the minds of finance industry executives and regulators was the future role of stablecoins and tokenized assets in the emerging era of programmable money.
Stablecoins are digital assets pegged to fiat currency, typically the U.S. dollar. They are designed to enable low-volatility and safe transactions in the crypto ecosystem.
The digital currency received a major boost last year with passage of the Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins or GENIUS Act, which standardized stablecoin rules across issuers and focused on reserve transparency and interoperability. However, when Congress attempted to set reserve requirements, audit standards and registration routes for stablecoins as part of the Clarity for Payment Stablecoins Act earlier this month, the bill failed passage in the U.S. Senate.
“This is a step backwards for our industry,” Ji Hun Kim, chief executive of the Crypto Council for Innovation, said during the Federal Reserve conference. “There’s going to be a lot more work in regulatory agencies to fill the gap.”
Support for tokenized assets
Despite the perceived setback for stablecoins, some leaders in the DeFi industry offered a different perspective, driven by the belief that a safer route for programmable money involved tokenized assets. While stablecoins can be issued by nonbanks with federal or state charters, tokenized deposits are digital representations of actual commercial bank money backed by FDIC insurance.
“I don’t see stablecoins as a future for retail payments,” Greg Baer, president and CEO of the Bank Policy Institute, said during one panel session. “The obvious alternative is tokenized deposits.”
An example of the ways that fledgling DeFi companies are seeking to bridge traditional finance, or TradFi, with tokenized systems is Custodia, a special-purpose depository formed to serve as a compliant link between the U.S. dollar payments system and digital assets. In June, Custodia unveiled a bank-architected token sub-ledger called Hazel Network, designed to safely bridge traditional banking with tokenized systems.
Hazel Network creates a frictionless, programmatic path for stablecoins to come back to the originating bank as tokenized deposits, thereby reducing fears that dollar stablecoins, with no bank account behind them, could drain traditional financial institution reserves.
“Tokenized deposits are going to eat stablecoins’ lunch,” Caitlin Long, founder and CEO of Custodia Bank, said during a panel session last week.
AI agents as payers and shoppers
While the financial world sorts out the impact of stablecoins vs. tokenized deposits, it must also deal with the growing influence of AI. This month saw the U.S. debut of Muse, a personal AI agent designed by Meta Platforms Inc., which can make purchases for a user via a new kind of payment infrastructure built by Stripe Inc.
The AI agent topped 730,000 downloads within five days, and surpassed OpenAI Group PBC’s chatbot as the most popular free app on the App Store. Finance executives are mindful that agents such as Muse could have a significant impact on their industry.
“Muse is taking something incredibly detailed, such as agents, and making it stupidly simple,” said Robert Bench, co-founder and CEO of Radius Inc. “They are going to tilt the space.”
How AI agents affect the financial world will be shaped by their dual role as a payments enabler and shopper. In August, the enterprise payments infrastructure provider Rain Inc. announced the launch of the Agentic Payments Alliance, a coalition of 26 founding members that included Visa and Mastercard. Rain facilitates agentic payments through its Agent Control Layer that was unveiled in June.
Agents running on Rain’s platform currently execute travel bookings, software subscriptions, end-to-end procurement workflows and cross-border money transfers. “There’s emerging greenspace here,” said Rain CEO Farooq Malik.
Questions around accountability
The broader implications of agentic AI as a shopper are still to be determined within the finance industry, but markets are already reacting. The launch of Meta Muse triggered a selloff in banking stocks this month, as investors reacted to fears that agentic AI could change the levers of shopping power.
“You will be able to tell your agent to maximize your yield,” said the Bank Policy Institute’s Baer. “It will challenge the banking industry.”
One factor that could slow the effect of AI on certain sectors of the financial industry is that building effective shopping agents is not an easy task. Last week, online retail giant Amazon.com Inc. signaled its interest with the introduction of a new agentic artificial intelligence service for third-party sellers on its main e-commerce site. Amazon also booted Muse off its platform, expressing concerns over customer security and user experience.
“Shopping is much more difficult, it’s a much more subjective determination,” said Brendan Woodbury, senior manager of payments policy at Amazon. “It’s harder to do a shopping agent well.”
There is also a growing debate over accountability for AI agents, whether that involves payments or shopping. Last week, a group of banks, including Bank of America and Capital One, issued a warning that agents for online shopping could increase the risk of scams, fraud and data privacy breaches affecting consumers.
“You have to answer the question for every transaction of who’s accountable,” said Sebastian Gunningham, CEO of money transfer platform provider Remitly Global Inc. “When you give that over to agents, that’s going to be a super-interesting question to answer.”
Building acceptance and plumbing
A subtext running through the dialogue at the Federal Reserve conference in Philadelphia this week was the friction between the TradFi world and the burgeoning DeFi community.
Questions around the role of stablecoins and their place in the global payment ecosystem persist. A study by Flagship Advisory Partners earlier this year found that only 5% of U.S. adults own stablecoins and merchant acceptance of the digital currency hovered around 6%.
“I see ourselves twisting into a pretzel to explain to someone in Argentina whether this is a dollar or not,” Gunningham said. “Is the stablecoin what they want? That bridge has to be crossed.”
There are also issues around the ability of existing financial infrastructure to support a new paradigm for decentralized finance and autonomous decision-makers. Traditional banking rails pause payment settlements on national holidays and over weekends, yet Rain has claimed to be the first fintech company to settle Visa card transactions seven days a week.
“We need to be talking about the future of plumbing,” said Sharplink’s Chalom. “The current rails don’t support it.”
Despite significant progress in gaining regulatory approval for cryptocurrency transactions, some industry figures remain concerned that the premise of a digital financial system for empowering people to lend, borrow, trade and earn interest without banks or middlemen is being lost in the shuffle. This month’s Congressional rejection of the Clarity Act may have been the best thing for the cryptocurrency world, according to Jai Massari, co-founder and chief legal officer of Lightspark Inc. and a lecturer at the Stanford Law School.
“Clarity was lowering the drawbridge so traditional finance would storm the crypto castle,” Massari said. “The crypto industry is not done yet and they have something meaningful to build.”
